text: work began soon after Trinity, with operations spanning from 1963–2004. Through continuous R&D, upgrades during 41 years of radiography have included several beam energy improvements, inclusion of graded collimators, the move to digital cameras, and a rudimentary dual-pulse capability. The use of LIAs for radiography was pioneered at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) in the late 1970s and resulted in the construction of the Flash X-Ray (FXR) machine in 1983. Due to the success of FXR, the initial DARHT accelerators were designed on the same basic LIA architecture. Improvements to the LIA technology on the DARHT accelerators provided a smaller and more consistent beam spot size and, coupled with more advanced GRCs, have been able to dramatically improve penetrating radiographic im- age quality. In 2004, PHERMEX was decommissioned based on the advancements made at DARHT and the age of the PHERMEX equipment. In 2010, the beam pulsing capability on A2 provided vastly improved time-resolved implosion data compared to PHERMEX and ushered in the modern era of hydrodynamic testing. Throughout the lifetime of DARHT, a broad suite of complementary diagnostics has been implemented and continuously improved, such that the DARHT diagnostics system is the centerpiece of the nation’s hydrotest program. Based on the successes of FXR and DARHT, the next generation of radiographic capability—Scorpius—is under con- struction in the Principal Underground Laboratory for Subcritical Experiments (PULSE) Complex at the Nevada Na- tional Security Site (NNSS). The primary use of Scorpius will be to provide late-time radiography (similar to DARHT) on subcritical experiments (SCEs) that contain fissile materials. With the commissioning of Scorpius in the latter part of this decade, the NNSA complex will have a comprehensive suite of penetrating radiographic capabilities to meet the mission need. Each facility—FXR, DARHT, and Scorpius—fills a critical and unique niche for the complex and all are used cooperatively to provide essential experimental data to support the evolving stockpile (see infographic on pages 10–11). The DARHT Complex is a comprehensive system of facilities and machines that provides a broad suite of diagnostic capabilities, and resulting datasets, for complex static (accelerator) and dynamic (high explosive [HE]) experiments. The DARHT Complex includes 12 major facilities, totaling 139,000 square feet, with an average age of 25 years. Building 183, constructed 61 years ago, is the oldest in the DARHT Complex. There are currently seven additional facilities in various planning stages that are collocated at Technical Area 15 (TA-15) to support DARHT operations, engineering, maintenance, repair, research, and development. These facilities include laboratories, high bays, an HE–prep room, storage areas, and offices. With oversimplification, machines include LIAs, accelerator component test stands, safety systems, GRC systems, laser systems, VCSs, vessel cleanout equipment, and vessel repair apparatus. Near-term projects include the Vessel Repair Facility, DARHT critical spares warehouse storage, and additional office space for technical staff. Mid-term projects include dedicated workspace for vessel inspection and staging. Advancements to the DARHT firing site optics room and to the Radiographic Support Lab (RSL) are planned for the long term.
